claims.text: A minor substitution with a transition metal having a substantially different atomic radius will improve glass-forming ability in a phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloy.
The same minor substitution will improve the thermal stability of the resulting amorphous phase.
An addition on the order of 1–2 at% is an appropriate concentration for the intervention.
The added species should be a transition metal whose atomic radius differs substantially from those of the existing constituents.
Rapid cooling, such as melt spinning or laser ablation, is required to bypass crystallization.
A sufficient atomic-radius mismatch induces local strain.
The intervention should improve the alloy only when the substitution does not cause phase segregation.
Elements with radii too similar to those of the existing constituents will produce insufficient mismatch and little or no improvement in glass formation.
An excessively large atomic-size mismatch may cause phase separation or excessive inhomogeneity.
Increased local atomic-size mismatch perturbs regular atomic packing.
Perturbation from atomic-size mismatch increases the energy barrier to crystal nucleation.
Atomic-size mismatch slows atomic diffusion and rearrangement.
The substitution deepens the eutectic character of the alloy by changing its free-energy landscape.
The substitution promotes higher configurational entropy.
Atomic-radius variability increases melt viscosity.
The resulting packing disruption and viscosity hinder crystal nucleation and growth during quenching.
The substitution elevates the activation-energy barrier for crystallization upon heating.
The substituted alloy will have a lower critical cooling rate for glass formation than the baseline alloy.
The substituted alloy will have a higher crystallization-onset temperature than the baseline alloy.
The magnitude of any improvement will depend sensitively on the selected atomic radii and concentrations.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis describes substitution of a transition metal, which implies replacing an existing constituent, whereas the intervention and experiment describe adding an additional dopant. These operations produce different final compositions.
